The network UI required either an aggressive zoom-and-pan model (which interfered with mobile touch gestures) or a compressed grid (which removed the topology decisions). After two iterations we accepted that the design and the platform were fighting each other, and committed to a Steam-only release. This is the design choice the launch is built on.

The economy assumes persistent saves and long-form runs. Modular tower loadouts only pay off across a campaign of missions — the third mission expects you to have committed to a network philosophy in the first two. Browser sessions are too disposable for that arc. Steam saves it cleanly; the web build would have either lost it on tab close or required a Firestore-backed save system that doesn't match how the rest of the catalogue treats persistence.

How Flux Tower Defense sits next to the platform's web TDs

ArcadeDeck's web catalogue already has two tower defenses: Polygon Invasion TD (chokepoint-and-tower-mix shape, 7-15 minute runs, depth-first leaderboard) and Mythic Defender: Heroes Returns (deck-driven, 25-40 minute runs, deeper meta layer). Flux Tower Defense is the third shape of the genre we're shipping: network-driven, multi-mission campaign, no procedural draw or wave-by-wave variance — just deliberate topology.

The three TDs answer different questions:

  • Polygon Invasion TD (web): can you read the map fast and place the right tower at the right pinch in seven minutes?
  • Mythic Defender (web): can you build a fight around the hand you've drawn, knowing tomorrow's draw will be different?
  • Flux Tower Defense (Steam): can you design a network that holds up under wave-shape changes you can't predict from turn one?

None of the three is a strict upgrade of the other two. The same player can prefer different shapes in different moods. If the seven-minute drive-by is what you want, the web TDs are built for that; Flux Tower Defense is the long-form sit-down option that lives on Steam because that's where the long-form sit-down lives.

What the web edition does still get

Three things, none of them gameplay.

A linked storefront from the platform sidebar. A small Steam icon appears in the ArcadeDeck navbar TD section that links out to the storefront. No popup, no overlay, no upsell screen. If you only ever play the web TDs, your experience does not change.

A future strategy companion post. Once the Steam-side leaderboards have a few weeks of data, we'll publish a network-design deep-dive here — the same kind of analysis the Galaxy Launch design post did for the idle-game tuning. It will be readable by anyone, useful primarily to players who own the Steam build, and the kind of long-form design writing this devlog exists for.

A wishlist nudge in the next monthly Hall of Fame recap. One line, no banner. Wishlists drive Steam's launch-window algorithm more than any other signal, and the players who follow this devlog are the audience most likely to enjoy the game. That's not cross-promotion, it's matchmaking.

Concrete things that actually help a Steam launch

If you've enjoyed the platform's TDs and want to support this one specifically: (1) wishlist on the Steam page — that's the single biggest visibility lever during launch week; (2) if you buy and play, leave a review even if it's short — Steam's discovery surfaces review-count thresholds more than star averages; (3) tag bug reports or balance feedback [FLUX] when you mail help@arcadedeck.net so it routes faster.

Why ship a Steam-only title at all

Two reasons, in order.

First, the catalogue should reflect what genres deserve, not what platform constraints allow. ArcadeDeck's identity is small, original browser games tuned to short sessions. That identity is real and we don't intend to dilute it — Polygon Invasion TD and Mythic Defender are exactly the kind of TDs the web platform was built for. But a network-driven TD is also a real shape of the genre, and refusing to ship it because it doesn't fit the web format would have meant either pretending it didn't exist or compromising the design until it did. Steam exists; it's the right home for this build; ship it there.

Second, parallel platforms compound rather than cannibalise. Void Survivor's Steam launch hasn't drained players from the web edition — both editions are growing independently. The audiences overlap less than you'd guess: web players are largely casual or seven-minute-window players; Steam players largely came for the long session. Flux Tower Defense gives the Steam side a second title that doesn't exist on the web, which both diversifies the Steam-side catalogue and gives the web players something to wishlist that they couldn't have played in a browser anyway.

Refusing to ship a network-driven TD because it didn't fit the web format would have meant either pretending it didn't exist or compromising the design until it did.

Two opening-game habits, since this is a TD post

If you wishlist and pick the game up at launch, two habits will save you the first three failed missions.

1. Build the network before you build the firepower

The first-instinct play is to drop a strong tower at the first chokepoint and route flux to it. It works for the first wave. By the third wave, you're starving the rest of the network and the next tower you want to place can't be powered. The right opening is two or three relays placed for routing, then towers placed inside the routed footprint. Network first, damage second.

2. Plan for a wave-shape change at the first boss

Boss waves don't just bump HP — they shift the enemy mix. A pure-plasma network optimised for the wave-3 swarm will leak on the wave-5 boss because the boss class resists plasma. Keep one tower slot flex-loaded with a different flux type, even if it's slightly under-tuned for the current wave. The flex slot pays for itself on the first wave-shape change and continues to pay across the run.

What's next

Two things on the immediate roadmap. First, a post-launch patch responding to the first week of telemetry — the launch build is balanced from internal playtest data, and the public data will reveal at least one mission that needs softening and one that needs hardening. Patch notes for that will land on this devlog and on the Steam community page. Second, the network-design deep-dive mentioned above, once there's enough leaderboard data to draw real conclusions about how players are actually routing.

The Hall of Fame cycle on the web platform is unaffected — Flux Tower Defense scores live on Steam's leaderboard, not on the ArcadeDeck global board. The May-June web cycle runs as scheduled, and the next monthly recap will mention the launch in a single line without restructuring around it.

Wishlist, play, or just browse

Storefront link, again, for convenience: store.steampowered.com/app/4645330/Flux_Tower_Defense. If you're new to the platform and curious what the web TDs play like before committing to a Steam purchase, Polygon Invasion TD is the closest in tone (deliberate placement, chokepoint reads) and Mythic Defender is the closest in depth (longer sessions, deeper meta).

Bug reports and feedback go to help@arcadedeck.net — tag the subject [FLUX] for routing. The most useful reports name a specific mission and a specific decision ("the routing constraint in mission 4 felt unsolvable because…") rather than general impressions.

Network up. Flux routed. See you on Steam.

title: Neon Stack Launches: One-Tap Tower Stacking, Blocks + Combo Scoring
author: ArcadeDeck Team
coverImageAlt: Neon Stack key art — a glowing block descending onto a tall tower of luminous stacked blocks against a synthwave city skyline.
excerpt: Neon Stack is live — a one-tap neon tower-stacking game with a dual-sort leaderboard that ranks blocks stacked first and best combo as the tiebreaker. Launch notes plus three habits that separate first-session players from leaderboard climbers.
content:
Neon Stack is live on ArcadeDeck. It is the platform's newest arcade title and its purest test of timing: one block slides back and forth above a rising tower, you tap to drop it, and the only thing between you and a record is the millisecond you release. The leaderboard sorts by Blocks Stacked first and Best Combo as the secondary tiebreaker — so a clean run of perfect aligns always outranks a sloppy tower of the same height. That single rule colours every decision below.

Where to play

Launch the game from the Neon Stack page. One input does everything — mouse click, screen tap, or spacebar drops the block. No login required: enter a nickname before your first run and scores submit to the global board automatically. It plays identically on desktop and mobile.

What's actually shipping

The launch build is the full core loop: a glowing block that slides above your tower at a constant speed, a tower that rises one block at a time, and an overhang-shear system that narrows your platform every time you miss dead-centre. Land a block flush over the one below and the next block keeps full width; land it short and the part hanging past the edge shears off, leaving you a narrower target. There is no timer and no acceleration — the run ends when the platform gets too thin to land on. Both desktop and touch are first-class inputs, and the one-tap design means the game plays the same on a phone as it does at a keyboard.

Why a dual-sort leaderboard for a stacking game

A pure height leaderboard would have been the obvious call. We didn't ship it because it would have flattened the game in exactly one direction: taller equals better, full stop, and the cleanest way to go tall is to grind survivable-but-sloppy drops until the platform is a sliver. Height alone rewards grinding, not precision.

The dual sort fixes that. Blocks Stacked is still primary — height is the headline number, and the player who builds taller wins ties going up the board. But when two runs reach the same height, the player with the longer best-combo streak wins. Best combo is the longest unbroken chain of perfect aligns in a run, so the tiebreaker rewards the player who built clean, not just high. The implication is concrete: chasing a perfect align is worth it even when a sloppy drop would keep you alive, because the combo you bank is the thing that breaks ties at the top of the board.

What this means for your first submissions

Don't optimise for height alone. A 60-block tower with a best combo of 8 will lose ties to a 60-block tower with a best combo of 22. If a drop would break your chain to gain almost nothing, holding the same height with the streak intact is often the better result.

Three habits that separate first-session players from leaderboard climbers

Most new players topple somewhere between 15 and 25 blocks on their first few runs, climb into the 40s once the rhythm clicks, and plateau there until they change how they look at the block. Three habits break the plateau.

1. Watch the edge, not the centre

The instinct is to track the middle of the sliding block and line it up with the middle of the tower. It feels right and it is slower than the alternative. The overhang is always sheared from the edge, so the edge is where the error actually shows up — and your eyes track a moving edge faster than they track a moving centre. Lock your focus on the trailing edge of the block and release as it crosses the edge of the platform below. Players who switch their focus point routinely report their best height jumping in a single session.

2. Tap on the beat — it's a rhythm game wearing a stacking game's clothes

The block's sliding speed never changes through a run. That single fact rewrites the optimal strategy: you are not reacting to each block, you are keeping a beat. The block crosses the centre of the tower on a fixed cadence, so the winning move is to find that cadence in the first few drops and then tap on it rather than eyeball every block fresh. Reacting is noisy and panicky; tapping on the beat is steady and repeatable. Once the rhythm clicks, the game stops feeling like a reflex test and starts feeling like holding a tempo.

3. Protect your width like it's the score

A perfect align keeps your platform at full width, but it never hands width back. The tower can only get narrower, never wider — which means every sloppy drop is a permanent tax on every drop after it. One greedy landing that leaves you a sliver effectively ends the run two or three blocks later, when that sliver becomes impossible to hit. Width is the resource you are actually managing; height is just what it buys you. Treat a near-miss that costs half your platform as the mistake it is, even though the run technically survives it.

Quick rule of thumb

Caught between a risky drop that might be perfect and a safe drop you know will shear a chunk? Wait for the beat instead of committing on instinct. The safe-but-sloppy drop narrows your platform and breaks your combo — on a dual-sort board, that's the worst of both worlds.

Why this fits the platform shape

ArcadeDeck's arcade catalogue already leans on the vertical screen. Skyfall is timer-driven and survival-shaped; Just Jump is rhythm built around a single repeating jump; Falling Dodger is pattern-reading around continuous spatial dodges. Neon Stack is the fourth shape: pure timing precision around a single committed input, where the challenge is not survival or dodging but the exact moment of release. Four games can share a vertical screen and still be four different skills.

The pitch we tested internally was one sentence: "how high can you build, and how cleanly?" Both halves had to matter independently, or the game would collapse into a height-grind within a week of launch. The dual-sort leaderboard is what makes both halves count — without the best-combo tiebreaker, the "how cleanly" half would have evaporated and Neon Stack would have been a worse version of every stacking game that came before it.

What we're watching post-launch

Two things on the immediate radar. First, the height-to-combo ratio in the top-10 slots. If everyone converges on a similar ratio, the dual sort isn't doing the strategic work we built it for and we'll weight best combo more heavily. If the top ranks spread across a range — some players grinding height, some chasing perfect chains — the design is healthy and we leave it alone. Second, where players topple on their first three runs. If the median first run ends under 15 blocks, the opening rhythm is harder to find than it should be and we'll look at the early tempo. Patch notes for any tuning land here.

A 60-block tower with a best combo of 8 loses ties to a 60-block tower with a best combo of 22. That single rule shapes the whole game.

Get on the board

The leaderboard is empty as of launch — early entries set the bar for the June-July Hall of Fame archive. If you crack the top three this week, expect a feature in the next monthly recap. Bug reports and tuning feedback go to help@arcadedeck.net; the most useful reports name a specific height and what broke the run ("the rhythm felt off around block 40 because…") rather than general impressions.

One block. One tap. One tempo. See how high the signal climbs.

title: Kingdom of Ashes - Fallen Era Lands on Steam
author: ArcadeDeck Team
coverImageAlt: Kingdom of Ashes - Fallen Era Steam key art — a hooded survivor cradling three glowing elemental orbs in fire, frost, and shadow before a burning ruined castle under an ember-streaked sky.
excerpt: Kingdom of Ashes - Fallen Era is now on Steam — a single-player roguelike deck-builder where you draft cards, chain elemental resonances, and spend Ash at the Forge across procedural runs. Storefront link, what's in the launch build, and how it sits next to the franchise's web games.
content:
Kingdom of Ashes - Fallen Era is live on Steam. The store page is up, the build is shipping, and the kingdom is waiting to be retaken one run at a time. This is the latest ArcadeDeck title to ship a full PC release — joining 40th Century: Void Survivor and Flux Tower Defense on Steam — and the first entry in the Kingdom of Ashes universe built from the ground up as a single-player roguelike deck-builder. There is no browser edition of this one: the full game lives on Steam. This post is the announcement, the design pitch, and an honest note on how it sits next to the franchise's web titles.

Storefront: store.steampowered.com/app/4732700

TL;DR

New single-player roguelike deck-builder on Steam, app ID 4732700, released June 4. Draft cards, chain elemental resonances, push through procedural maps of battles, shrines, and bosses, then spend Ash at the Forge for permanent upgrades. Eight heroes, brutal Ascension tiers, a relic codex, localized in 10 languages. Steam only — no web edition. Windows, single-player, one-time purchase (CDN$ 12.25; regional pricing applies).

The pitch in one paragraph

The night the kingdom fell, you alone survived. From the ashes of a broken throne you forge a deck, master the elements, and march back into the dark to face the Lord of Shadows. Fallen Era is a roguelike deck-builder in the classic shape — draft cards into a run-specific deck, fight turn-based encounters across a branching procedural map, and chain elemental resonances to turn a handful of cheap cards into a combo that deletes a boss. Lose, learn, forge, return. The kingdom is ash; the crown is still down there.

What's actually in the launch build

This is a full release, not an Early Access slice. Highlights:

  • Roguelike deck-building. Every run is a fresh deck drafted from rewards, shrines, and shops. The cards you skip matter as much as the ones you take — a bloated deck dilutes the combo you're trying to assemble.
  • Eight fallen heroes. Each hero starts with a distinct core deck and identity, so the same map plays differently depending on who you march in with.
  • Elemental resonance. The core mechanic. Cards carry elements, and chaining matching elements in sequence triggers resonance effects that scale far past raw card stats. The skill ceiling lives in sequencing, not just card quality.
  • Procedural run maps. Branching paths of battles, shrines, elite fights, and bosses. Route choice is a real decision — the safe path and the greedy path each cost you something different.
  • Living encounter nodes. Map nodes aren't only fights; shrines, events, and choices reshape your deck mid-run.
  • Persistent meta-progression — the Forge. Each run pays out Ash, spent at the Forge for permanent upgrades that carry between attempts. This is the run-to-run layer that turns a losing streak into a slow climb.
  • Ascension tiers. Brutal difficulty modifiers for players who've cleared the base game and want the run to fight back harder.
  • Relic codex. Stackable relics with a catalogue that fills in as you discover them — soft progression for completionists.
  • Localized in 10 languages. The same localization discipline the web catalogue runs on.

Why a Steam release, and no web edition

The Kingdom of Ashes name already lives on ArcadeDeck's web catalogue — Dice War and Endless War are both free, browser-native, and tuned to the platform's seven-minute median session. Fallen Era is deliberately not that. A roguelike deck-builder lives or dies on run length and persistent progression, and neither fits a disposable browser tab cleanly. Three concrete reasons drove the Steam-only call.

Run length doesn't match the platform's median. A full Fallen Era run — drafting a deck, routing a procedural map, clearing the boss gauntlet — runs well past the seven-minute window the web catalogue is built around. Compressing it would have meant cutting either the deck depth or the map variety, and neither cut survived prototyping.

The meta-progression assumes persistent saves. The Forge, the Ash economy, the relic codex, and Ascension tiers only pay off across many runs. Browser sessions are too disposable for that arc without a Firestore-backed save layer that doesn't match how the rest of the catalogue treats persistence. Steam saves it cleanly.

Web Hall of Fame is separate

Fallen Era is single-player and lives entirely on Steam. Its progress, achievements, and Ascension clears do not flow into the ArcadeDeck global leaderboard or the monthly Hall of Fame cycle — that remains a web-catalogue system. If you only play on Steam, your runs don't count toward the Hall of Fame, and that's a deliberate boundary, not a bug.

The deck-builder shape rewards a sit-down session. Reading a hand, planning a resonance chain, weighing a map fork — that's a lean-in, take-your-time loop, not a quick-strike one. Steam is where the long sit-down lives.

How it sits next to the Kingdom of Ashes web games

The franchise now spans four distinct shapes, and none is a strict upgrade of the others:

  • Kingdom of Ashes - Dice War (web): the dice-deck roguelike — chapter-based runs driven by dice rather than cards. Free, browser, leaderboard.
  • Kingdom of Ashes - Endless War (web): the wave-survival strategy entry. Free, browser, leaderboard.
  • Vault of Ashes: Fallen Era (web): the grid auto-battler — build a loadout, watch it fight. Same fallen-era setting, a completely different verb.
  • Kingdom of Ashes - Fallen Era (Steam): the deck-builder — the long-form, sit-down, run-based entry that doesn't fit a browser tab.

If you've enjoyed the franchise's web titles and want a deeper, longer version of the same world, the Steam build is built for exactly that player. If the seven-minute browser session is what you want, the web entries are still free and still live.

Two opening-run habits for new players

If you pick it up, two habits will save you the first few failed runs.

1. Keep your deck thin

The beginner instinct is to take every card on offer. It's a trap. A roguelike deck-builder wins by consistency — the smaller your deck, the more reliably you draw the resonance chain you've been building. Skip cards that don't serve your element plan, even good ones. A lean deck that always combos beats a fat deck that only sometimes does.

2. Commit to a resonance early, then forge between runs

Decide which element your run is built around in the first few fights and draft toward it — splitting across three elements gives you a hand that never resonates. And when you lose (you will, early), spend your Ash at the Forge before the next attempt. The meta-progression is the difference between run five and run twenty-five; ignoring it is the most common way new players stall. Losing isn't the end of the run loop — it's the currency for the next one.

If you want to support the launch

The most useful actions, in rough order:

  1. Buy and play if the pitch lands — it's a one-time purchase on the store page.
  2. Leave a review, even a short one. Steam's discovery surfaces review-count thresholds more than star averages, especially during a launch window.
  3. Wishlist if you're not ready to buy — wishlists still feed the storefront's visibility algorithm.
  4. Tell us what's off. Mail help@arcadedeck.net and tag the subject [ASHES] so it routes fast. The most useful reports are specific ("the third boss feels unwinnable with a frost deck because…") rather than general impressions.

A note on the art

For transparency, and matching the disclosure on the Steam page: Fallen Era's visuals are AI-assisted — finalized during development and shipped as static assets. We'd rather say so plainly here than leave it unstated.

What's next

Two things on the immediate roadmap. First, a post-launch balance pass responding to the first weeks of player data — a deck-builder always ships with at least one over-tuned card and one dead one, and the public meta surfaces them faster than any internal playtest. Second, the franchise's web entries stay on their own cadence; the Steam launch is additive and doesn't pull development off the browser titles. Patch notes for Fallen Era land on the Steam community page; anything that affects the web franchise lands here.

Storefront link, once more: store.steampowered.com/app/4732700/Kingdom_of_Ashes__Fallen_Era. Forge a deck. Master the elements. Take the kingdom back.

title: AshenKeys Launch: Typing Is the Weapon, Regeneration Is the Wall
author: ArcadeDeck Team
coverImageAlt: AshenKeys key art — glowing runic keys and ember-lit script against the dark of a keep’s lower levels.
excerpt: AshenKeys is live: an incremental typed on the whole keyboard, with no health bar and no death. Why enemy regeneration is the entire difficulty curve, how combo drives everything, and what to do in your first session.
content:
AshenKeys is live on ArcadeDeck. It is an incremental played on the whole keyboard: every printable key is a basic strike, and typing a skill’s keyword casts it — type "fire" and Fireball lands, type "frost" and the foe freezes over. There is no health bar on your side, nothing attacks you, and there is no defeat screen. What stands between you and the next level is arithmetic: every enemy regenerates a fixed amount of health per second, and if your damage per second sits under that number, the bar refills faster than you empty it.

Where to play

Launch it from the AshenKeys page. It is PC only — a physical keyboard is the controller, so there is nothing to tap on a phone. No login: your progress saves in your own browser, and the left rail opens Skill Mastery, Attack Mastery, Passives and Ascension while Escape closes whatever overlay is open.

What is actually shipping

The launch build is the full loop. Forty-six skills across eight elements, each with its own keyword, sprite and status effect — burn, chill, poison, curse, bleed, a shock that arcs and a smite that bursts. A hundred hand-painted foes climb from fodder to elites, with a boss every tenth level that you engage by typing its name from the incantation on screen. Four upgrade economies run underneath all of it, an ascension prestige sits on top, and the level curve is procedural and does not end.

Why we took the player health bar out

The first prototype had one. It was the least interesting number on the screen. In a keyboard-driven clicker, damage taken is not a decision you make — it is a tax on how long you were away from the keys, and the honest player response to it is to stop experimenting and start playing safe. Worse, it made failure a rewind: you lose, you repeat ground you already covered, and the game spends your time telling you something it already told you.

So we cut it. You cannot die, and nothing down there is trying to kill you. The pressure in AshenKeys is entirely economic: a foe you cannot out-damage costs you time, not a run. That single removal is what lets the game be honest about its actual difficulty curve, which was never combat in the first place.

The regeneration wall is the difficulty curve

Every enemy in the game regenerates a fixed amount of health per second. That is the whole fail state. Push a foe whose regeneration outpaces your damage and the bar climbs back up while you hit it — the fight does not end in defeat, it stalls, and the readout under the fight tells you so by putting your rolling DPS next to the enemy’s regeneration. You are not guessing whether you are close. You can see exactly how far short you are.

We like this for a reason that took a while to articulate internally: a stall is a legible instruction and a death is not. A death screen tells you that you failed. A refilling health bar tells you roughly how much more damage per second you need, and points at the four screens where you go get it. A wall you can measure is a goal; a wall you cannot measure is a grind.

If the bar keeps refilling, that is not bad luck

It is the game’s only fail state, working as designed. Do not keep swinging at a stalled foe — spend points on damage, or chill the target. Chill cuts an enemy’s regeneration directly, which makes a frost skill in your deck a lockpick for walls you cannot yet out-damage.

Combo is the engine, and it decays

Hits landed close together stack a combo counter, and combo is not a small bonus on the side — it is the multiplier the entire build routes through. It raises crit chance and double-strike chance on every hit, ramps basic damage through Momentum, and scales skill hits on a separate track on top of that. Pushed far enough, both chances cap past 100% and strikes start landing three and four at a time.

Then you stop typing and the whole thing decays to zero. That is deliberate. In a game with no death, idling has to cost something, or the optimal strategy collapses into walking away from the keyboard. Combo decay is the only clock in AshenKeys, and it is the reason a session has a rhythm instead of a plateau. Early on, the crit and double-strike chance your combo is holding for you is worth more than any single upgrade you could buy by stopping to shop.

A death screen tells you that you failed. A refilling health bar tells you how much more damage per second you need, and points at where to get it.

Ten equipped, three shown, never quite what you just cast

You equip up to ten skills. The fight shows three of them at a time as keywords in the cast slots, and casting one spends that slot, which immediately redraws from the rest of your deck. So your next cast is never reliably the one you just used — what you can do is a function of what your deck can offer, not of what your fingers memorised.

This is the part that most changes how the game reads after the first hour. A ten-skill deck with three visible slots is a hand, and building it is a real decision: stack one element for status pressure and the redraw keeps handing you the tool you want, or spread across eight and the slots become a rolling toolkit that always has an answer but rarely a stacked one.

Two behaviours per skill is what makes a deck a build

Every skill earns its own XP and its own levels, spent in a star-shaped tree unique to that skill: power and cooldown leaves, plus six behaviour points — Double, Overflow, Chaining, Echoing, Surging and Lingering. A skill can hold at most two of the six.

The cap is the most load-bearing rule in the game and the one we argued about longest. Without it, every skill converges on the same six-behaviour end state and a deck stops being a set of choices — it becomes ten copies of the same fully-upgraded button wearing different sprites. With it, Lingering plus Surging on one skill and Chaining on another are genuinely different objects, and the deck is a composition rather than a list.

Four economies feeding one hot path

Progress arrives on four separate tracks, and all of them cash out in the same place — the damage number you are measuring against that regeneration wall.

  1. Attack Mastery grows from your basic hits, so mashing is never wasted input even when your casts are on cooldown.
  2. Per-skill star trees grow from each skill’s own XP, which means the skills you actually play are the skills that get stronger.
  3. A passive taproot grows from drops, rewarding depth rather than activity.
  4. Ash arrives when you prestige, and buys the ascension tree that raises your floor for every run after it.

Four currencies could easily have been three too many. They survive because each one answers a different question about how you got stuck: too little raw output, the wrong skills levelled, not deep enough yet, or a floor that is simply too low and wants a reset.

Your first session, in order

The single most common opening mistake is fighting before building. A fresh save equips no skills at all, so the three cast slots read "not enough skills" and every key you press falls through to a basic strike — the game looks like a plain masher because, until you equip something, it is one.

  1. Open Skill Mastery and equip a deck first. Up to ten skills; their keywords start appearing in the cast slots immediately.
  2. Keep one frost skill in it. Chill cuts regeneration, which is a direct answer to the only thing that can stop you.
  3. Keep hitting. Combo decays on idle, and the bonuses it grants outweigh early upgrades.
  4. Read the DPS-versus-regeneration readout before you decide a foe is unfair. It is telling you which of the four trees to spend in.
  5. Type boss incantations carefully. Every tenth level opens with a name you must type to engage the fight, and typos are counted.

Why it is PC only

Most of the ArcadeDeck catalogue plays on both desktop and phone, and where a game can reasonably support touch we ship it that way — Neon Stack is one tap on either. AshenKeys cannot be. Basics, casts and boss incantations are all typed, and an on-screen keyboard would eat the screen the fight lives on while turning the game’s best feeling — a word struck cleanly landing as a blade — into hunting for letters. A worse version on more devices was not the trade we wanted.

How it sits next to the rest of the catalogue

ArcadeDeck already has incrementals. Galaxy Launch is an idle game about progression that keeps meaning something while you are away — we wrote about that problem at length in keeping idle progression meaningful. Entrepreneur Tycoon is accumulation with a simulation wrapped around it. 15s Click Challenge is the opposite extreme: fifteen seconds of pure input and no economy at all.

AshenKeys is the input-heavy corner of that same space. It rewards presence rather than patience, which is why combo decays and why there is no offline-earnings screen to check. It is an incremental you play with your hands, not one you check on.

What we are watching post-launch

Three things. First, where the first real regeneration wall lands — if most players stall before they have meaningfully used any of the four upgrade trees, the wall is teaching nothing and we will move it. Second, deck diversity under the two-behaviour cap: if the strongest decks all converge on the same pair on the same skill, the cap is not doing the work we built it for. Third, friction on boss incantations, which are the one place a typo costs you something and therefore the one place the typing conceit could turn from satisfying to irritating.

Bug reports and tuning notes go to help@arcadedeck.net — the useful ones name a level and what stalled ("wall at level 34 with a full shadow deck because…") rather than general impressions. Patch notes land here.

Nothing down there can hurt you. You are simply not strong enough yet, and the dark can wait longer than you can.

title: Barrack Defense Launch Notes: A Defense Game With No Towers
author: ArcadeDeck Team
coverImageAlt: Barrack Defense key art — training halls ringed around a central keep with armored units marching out toward the roads.
excerpt: Barrack Defense is live: your buildings never attack, they train units that fight on their own. Why barracks double as walls, how armor math decides every matchup, and an opening order for your first ten waves.
content:
Barrack Defense is live on ArcadeDeck, and it is a defense game with no towers in it. Nothing you build ever attacks anything. What you place are barracks; what fights for you are the soldiers, archers, knights, rogues, brutes, bombardiers and falconers those barracks train, who walk out on their own, pick their own targets and hold the ground you gave them. You decide what gets produced, where it is produced from, and what that costs. The units handle the rest.

Where to play

Launch it from the Barrack Defense page. PC only — it wants a mouse and a wide screen, because placement precision and right-click repair both assume one. Keys 1–7 pick a barrack type, 8 is the Frontier, U upgrades the selected type, F cycles 1×/2×/3× speed and Space pauses. Best wave and best score save in your own browser.

What is actually shipping

The launch build is the complete loop: seven barrack types with distinct damage roles, per-type upgrades with no level cap, ground and air waves, destructible and repairable buildings, and an endless wave curve with a boss every fifth wave and a mega-boss every tenth. From wave ten on, bosses bring their own air escort. There is no final wave and no victory screen — the run ends when the Center Command falls, and the only question is how far you got.

Your production line is standing on the battlefield

This is the rule that reframes the whole game, and most players find it on run three rather than run one. Every barrack is a building with hit points, sitting in the mud where the fighting happens. That makes placement two decisions at once: a barrack pushed out toward a lane is a factory and a wall, soaking the first hit before anything reaches the keep; a barrack tucked in behind is safe, and its units arrive late to every fight they are needed in.

Rams and gargoyles sharpen the trade by hitting barracks for double damage. They are not incidentally destructive — they come specifically for your training halls, because an army you cannot replace is an army already beaten. A defense that never loses a building is a defense that was probably built too far back. Losing halls on the front edge is not a mistake to be avoided; it is the cost of having units on the line when the wave lands, and right-click repair during the build phase is how you pay it cheaply.

Armor is the whole puzzle

Combat runs on real numbers rather than a rock-paper-scissors chart. Armor mitigates incoming physical damage as a fraction, which means it blunts many small hits far harder than a few big ones. Pierce damage halves the target’s armor. Magic damage ignores it completely. Bleed, slow and burn stack on top of all of it.

The practical consequence is the single most common new-player mistake in the game: a rogue’s fast four-damage flurry bounces off a plated tank while a brute’s one twenty-damage swing goes through nearly in full. Same total damage on paper, wildly different result on the field. Rogues are for swarms. Brutes and bombardiers are for anything wearing plate, and bombardiers are the reliable answer when the armored wave arrives clustered.

Wave 6 is where runs end

Flying imps arrive at wave 6 and ground-only melee cannot touch them — they fly straight over your wall of soldiers and knights, and the keep has no answer of its own. Get one Archer or Falconer hall up before wave 6, not during it. The air problem is trivially solved in advance and unsolvable once it is on top of you.

Eight seconds is the real decision window

Waves arrive in two phases: an eight-second build countdown with nothing on the field, then the assault itself. Everything you decide happens in those eight seconds — place a hall, repair a damaged one, sell a full-HP building for 50% back to reshape a lane, spend on the upgrade that raises a whole type at once.

That structure is why we did not build a pause-to-plan phase of unlimited length. A defense game that lets you think forever between waves turns into a spreadsheet, and one that never lets you think turns into reflex soup. Eight seconds is long enough to execute a plan you already have and short enough that you have to have made it during the previous fight. The build phase is for committing, not for deliberating.

Opening strategy: your first ten waves

Most first runs die somewhere between wave 6 and wave 12, and almost always for one of three reasons: no air coverage, too many buildings and no upgrades, or rogues thrown at armor. This order fixes all three.

  1. Soldiers first. At 40 gold they are the cheapest way to get bodies between the road and the keep, and bodies are what buys you time in the early waves.
  2. Buy your first upgrade before your fourth barrack. A Lv.2 type out-produces a second building of the same type for less gold — upgrades give +25% damage and HP plus faster spawns across every hall of that type, and they have no level cap.
  3. One Archer or Falconer up before wave 6. Non-negotiable. See the warning above.
  4. Read the wave preview and build the answer. Brutes and bombardiers for armored pushes, rogues for swarms, knights where you want something to stand still and hold.
  5. Repair during the build phase, not after. A right-click repair costs a fraction of a rebuild and scales to the health missing. Patching a hall at 30% is cheap; replacing it is not.
  6. When gold outpaces your buildable ring, plant a Frontier. It extends where you can build, and a second front is worth more than a fifth hall stacked on the keep.

Seven types and an expanding question

The roster is not a power ladder where the later unlocks replace the earlier ones. Each of the seven types answers a different kind of arrival: cheap bodies, ranged chip, a body that holds, a fast shredder for unarmored swarms, a heavy swing that ignores most mitigation, splash for a clustered armored push, and anti-air. Every enemy that shows up is a question about which of your seven answers it — and the answer keeps changing as the roster and the waves both grow.

That is also why per-type upgrades have no cap. A wide roster of Lv.1 halls loses to a deep run every time, but so does a single over-invested type the moment something arrives that it cannot hurt. The interesting decisions live between those two failure modes, and gold is the thing that forces the choice.

A defense that never loses a building is a defense that was probably built too far back.

Endless on purpose

There is no final wave. Enemies keep coming and keep scaling, arriving down one lane early and splitting across more roads as the run deepens, with the boss cadence marking every fifth and tenth wave. We considered a finite campaign and dropped it for the same reason the health bar came out of AshenKeys: a fixed end turns a defense game into a puzzle with a solution, and once the solution is known the building stops being interesting. An endless curve keeps the question open — not can you hold, but how long, and with what.

Where it sits in the ArcadeDeck defense catalogue

This is the fourth defense game on the platform and deliberately the least tower-shaped. Polygon Invasion TD is classic placement and range geometry (launch notes here). Mythic Defenders puts a card draft in front of the placement, which we dug into in card-driven tower defense design. Gate of Hell is survival pressure with waves closing from every direction.

Barrack Defense takes the one thing all three share — buildings that shoot — and removes it. What is left is a game about production, positioning and replacement rather than coverage and range, and it plays differently enough that the usual tower-defense instincts actively mislead for the first few runs.

What we are watching post-launch

Three things. First, wave 6: if the air spike is ending a majority of first runs, the imps are arriving before the game has taught anti-air rather than after. Second, whether the barracks-as-walls idea is landing — if most players build their whole ring at maximum distance from the roads and never lose a hall, the double damage on rams and gargoyles is not creating the trade we intended. Third, the upgrade-versus-expand curve: a Lv.2 type should beat a second hall early, and if that stops being true at any point on the curve, the numbers move.

Bug reports and balance notes go to help@arcadedeck.net. The useful ones name a wave and what broke ("lost the keep on wave 14 to the armored push because…") rather than general impressions. Patch notes land here.

The hall keeps counting. See how many waves you can make it count for.

title: Shadow Runner: The Free Chapter 1 Demo Ships the Whole Loop
author: ArcadeDeck Team
coverImageAlt: Shadow Runner key art — a katana-wielding runner mid-slash in a dark, collapsing corridor lit by neon signal light.
excerpt: Shadow Runner is playable on ArcadeDeck as the free Chapter 1 demo, with the full game on Steam. Why the demo cuts chapters instead of systems, how the three-phase combo actually works, and four habits for your first hour.
content:
Shadow Runner is playable on ArcadeDeck, and the Steam release is live. It is a side-scrolling katana action-roguelike about one runner, one blade and a descent with no retreat written into it — scripted waves on hand-built maps, an upgrade card after every clear, and a hub you come back to between chapters. The web build is the free Chapter 1 demo: the whole loop, stopped at the first landing.

Where to play

The demo runs in your browser on the Shadow Runner page — PC only, keyboard or gamepad, no touch controls. Defaults are arrows to move, Space to jump, Z to attack, X for super/dive/plunge, C to dash, S for your sub-weapon. Every button remaps in Settings. The full game is on Steam: store.steampowered.com/app/4984730/Shadow_Runner.

What is actually in the web demo

Chapter 1, The Corridor — three waves across the corridor maps — plus the tutorial, the hub, the shop, the equipment and inventory screens, the challenge arena and the entire meta progression layer. Gold, gear and Echo shrine upgrades persist between runs in your browser, so the roguelike loop is intact rather than simulated. You die, you bank what you earned, you come back stronger. The descent just stops at the first landing.

Why the demo is a slice of the loop, not a slice of the map

The easy version of a browser demo is a level: here is some content, the rest is behind a storefront link. We did not ship that, because a roguelike shown as one level is a roguelike with its best argument removed. The point of the genre is not the room you are standing in — it is that dying is a transaction, and the run after the death is measurably better armed than the one before it.

So the demo cuts chapters, not systems. The shop rolls a fresh card selection, the equipment NPC and the mannequin work, loot still drops with affixes and set bonuses, and the Echo shrine still converts run currency into permanent upgrades. What you are evaluating in the browser is the actual game, at a shallower depth — which is the only honest way to ask someone whether they want the other eleven chapters.

Do not mash Z

The light attack runs a three-phase combo, and the third hit is where the damage lives. Mashing drops you out of the rhythm and resets the chain, which is why a dropped combo costs more than a slow one. This is the single biggest gap between a first session and a fifth: the button is not a damage-per-second lever, it is a phrase with a cadence, and the game pays you for finishing the phrase.

Hit-pause and a short slow-motion beat land on every clean kill, so the feedback loop teaches the timing without a tutorial box explaining it. A combo that reads well is also a combo that landed — the feel and the math agree on purpose. If the hit-pause is not firing, you are mashing.

One button, three moves, depending on where you are

X is a super on the ground, a dive in the air and a plunge while falling. That is not a shortage of buttons; it is a way of making position the input. The dive carries through a target, which makes it an exit from a crowd rather than an opener on one — the most common early misuse is diving into a wave instead of out of it.

Dash sits on the same logic. It is an escape and a repositioning tool, not a movement key, and dive-cancel lets you rewrite your spacing mid-fight. Spend every charge travelling and you will have none the moment a wave closes from both sides.

Save a dash charge

Waves arrive in scripted groups and the field must be cleared before the next one spawns, which means you can read what is coming and hold a charge for it. A dash spent crossing the map is a dash you do not have when something closes on both sides — and that is the moment the demo kills most first-time runners.

Pact of Curses: opt-in difficulty that pays

Before a chapter starts you can take a Pact of Curses — accept penalties in exchange for stacked rewards, reshaping the rules of that specific run. It is the most interesting decision in the game and the one new players skip longest, which is backwards. Reward stacking compounds across a whole run, and Chapter 1 is exactly where a penalty costs you least. Take curses early, while the floor is forgiving and the compounding has the most room left to work.

Four habits for your first hour

  1. Finish the phrase. Three-phase combo, third hit carries the damage. Slow and complete beats fast and dropped.
  2. Hold a dash. Treat charges as emergency exits, not as a way to get across the room faster.
  3. Dive out, not in. X in the air carries through a target — it is how you break out of a crowd.
  4. Spend at the Echo shrine before the shop. Meta upgrades survive the run; shop cards do not. When gold is tight, the shrine is the purchase that is still there after you die.

The sub-weapon slot — drone, grenade, knife, disc, tether or skull — sits on top of all of it and is meant to be swapped to fit the run you are actually having rather than the run you planned. If your card draws pushed you toward crowd control, the disc and the tether are doing more than the knife is.

The demo cuts chapters, not systems. What you play in the browser is the real loop, at a shallower depth.

What the Steam release adds

Chapters 2 through 12, the Volcano and Underworld side campaigns, endless mode, the rest of the bestiary and the later bosses. Difficulty tiers go further too — Easy and Normal are picked at the title screen and each keeps its own save slot, and Nightmare unlocks later in the full release. The game ships with six in-game languages, English, Korean and Japanese among them.

On saves and scores, plainly

Demo progress does not carry into the Steam build. The browser demo saves to your own local storage; the Steam version keeps its own save on Steam Cloud. There is no web leaderboard — score and best wave stay in your browser and nothing is uploaded from this page. The Steam release pushes them to a Steam leaderboard instead. What transfers between the two is what your hands learned about the combo timing.

How it sits next to the rest of the catalogue

ArcadeDeck already has roguelikes, and this is a different axis of one. 40th Century Void Survivor is survival pressure and build snowball — we covered its own Steam launch in that write-up. Kingdom of Ashes - Fallen Era is turn-based deck-building where the decision happens before the damage does (launch notes here).

Shadow Runner is the expression corner. The roguelike layer decides what you are carrying; your hands decide what happens with it. That is why the combat is built around a combo with a rhythm and a movement kit with cancels, rather than around numbers that resolve on their own — and it is also why the demo needed the hub attached. A run you played well and a run you were built well for should feel different, and you cannot show that with one level.

If you want to support the launch

  1. Play the demo and tell us where it lost you. The most useful report names a wave and a moment ("wave 3 kills me every time when the group closes from both sides because…") rather than a general impression.
  2. Wishlist or review on Steam. Review counts and wishlists both feed storefront visibility far more than star averages do during a launch window.
  3. Mail help@arcadedeck.net with the subject tagged [RUNNER] so it routes fast.

What we are watching

Two things. First, whether players find the combo rhythm inside Chapter 1 or bounce off it — if most demo sessions end while still mashing, the tutorial is teaching the buttons but not the cadence, and that is a fixable problem on the web build. Second, Pact of Curses uptake: the system is designed to be taken early, and if almost nobody opts in during the demo, the pitch for it is not landing where players can see it.

Storefront link once more: store.steampowered.com/app/4984730/Shadow_Runner. The signal is already broken. There is only the next landing, and the thing waiting on it.

title: Fruit Frenzy v1.3: Shoot the Bombs, Read the Spin
author: ArcadeDeck Team
coverImageAlt: Fruit Frenzy key art — a glowing neon basket beneath a burst of watermelon, pineapple, cherries and bombs on a purple starfield.
excerpt: Fruit Frenzy v1.3 is live: a gun that pops bombs mid-air, a rare ammo crate, fruit that hops, brakes, skids and hovers, bombs that seek the basket, a HiDPI canvas, Japanese, and a mobile performance pass. Full patch notes and why each change happened.
content:
Fruit Frenzy v1.3 is live on the play page. It is the biggest change the game has had since launch: the basket now carries a gun, fruit has learned to hop, brake, skid and hover on the way down, and bombs have started steering toward you. The catcher you knew is still in there — slide under fruit, build the combo, keep your three lives — but from level 2 onward the sky is no longer a straight-line problem. Under the hood it also got a HiDPI canvas, a Japanese locale, pointer lock on PC and a performance pass that matters most on phones. This post is the full notes and the reasoning behind each change.

TL;DR

Click or tap to fire a bullet straight up. Shooting a bomb pops it for a point; shooting a fruit destroys it and costs a life. You bank 2 bullets and one reloads every ~1.5 seconds. A very rare ammo crate grows the bank to 4. Fruit now hops, brakes, skids and hovers; bombs seek the basket from level 2. A missed fruit counts the instant it clears the basket. Japanese added. Personal-best tiers on the play page reset to 300 / 1,000 / 2,000.

1. The gun

The single largest addition. Left-click on PC or tap on a phone fires one bullet straight up from the basket. It exists for exactly one target: bombs. A bullet that hits a bomb detonates it mid-air, pays 1 point, and counts as a bomb avoided for the achievement track. A bullet that hits a fruit destroys it, and destroying a fruit costs a life, the same as missing one.

That asymmetry is deliberate. The first prototype let you shoot anything, and within a few sessions the optimal play was to hose the whole sky and catch nothing. The basket became a gun turret with a scoring bug. Making a shot fruit cost a life turns every trigger pull into a read: is that thing falling toward me a bomb, and can I get a bullet under it before it lands? The gun is not a way to skip the catching game. It is a way to answer bombs you cannot dodge.

Ammo is the throttle. You bank two bullets, and one comes back roughly every 1.5 seconds. The two pips in the top-left of the panel show the state — the reloading pip fills up, and clicking on an empty bank rattles the pips red instead of firing. Two shots is enough to clear a bomb pair that lands together; it is not enough to clear a level-6 spawn wave, which is the point.

2. The ammo crate

Very rarely — about 0.6% of spawns, roughly one every three minutes at mid levels — a crate drifts down at 70% of normal speed with a cyan glow. Catching it does two things: it grows your bullet bank by one, up to a cap of four, and it refills the bank on the spot. Missing it costs nothing. Bullets pass straight through it, so you cannot accidentally shoot it.

It is the only pickup in the game that is free to miss, and that is on purpose. A crate that punished you for chasing it would be a trap dressed as a reward. Instead it is a pure upside detour: if the sky is clear enough to go get it, go get it, and a four-bullet bank turns the level-6 bomb rate into target practice.

3. Fruit that moves

Before v1.3 fruit fell in a handful of patterns — straight, drift, zigzag, bounce, accelerate, pendulum — and once you had seen each one you could catch it on autopilot. Four new movement types join the pool, and they are physics-shaped rather than pattern-shaped:

  • Hop. The fruit falls, hits an invisible floor somewhere in the upper half of the screen, bounces back up, then falls again. Some hop twice. The bounce speed is capped at 2.2× the fruit’s base speed so a hop is never faster than something you could have caught anyway.
  • Brake. Starts at 2.6× speed and bleeds it off with air friction down to about half. It looks like it will land long before it does.
  • Skid. A hard sideways shove that friction slowly kills. It arrives well to one side of where it spawned.
  • Hover. Stalls partway down, spins up for half a second to a second, then plunges. The spin is the tell — the faster it turns, the closer the drop.

None of these appear at level 1. Hop, brake and skid enter at level 2 with low weight and climb steadily; hover enters at level 3. By level 7 the straight-drop weight is a fifth of what it was at level 1, so the top of the curve is mostly fruit that is doing something. The old patterns did not go anywhere; they just share the pool.

4. Bombs that seek

From level 2, roughly 30% of bombs steer toward the basket. The steering is friction-damped — a seeking bomb leans into its turns and cannot snap sideways — so it is dodgeable, but dodging one that has already committed to your position is a coin flip. From level 3 a quarter of bombs bounce off the walls, and from level 4 some hover before dropping, with the same spin-up tell as fruit.

Seeking bombs and the gun shipped together because one needs the other. A bomb that hunts you would be unfair in a game where dodging is your only verb. A gun in a game where every bomb falls straight would be a toy. Together they make a decision: keep a bullet banked for the bomb that leans into you, and dodge the ones that do not.

A miss now counts sooner

Before v1.3 a missed fruit only cost a life once it left the bottom of the screen. Now it counts the instant the fruit clears the underside of the basket. The old rule let you sweep the basket under fruit that had already fallen past it, which looked like a catch and felt like a bug. Commit early instead of chasing.

5. Scoring and levels, unchanged

None of the economy moved. Every fruit is 1 point, or 2 once your combo reaches 3. Rare stars — about 4% of non-bomb spawns — pay 3. A shot bomb pays 1. Levels still advance on score at 10, 25, 45, 70, 100 and 140 points, from Novice to Myth; each step speeds the fall, thickens the spawn rate, raises the bomb chance from 10% at level 1 to 22% at level 7, and trims the basket a little. Combo is still the whole economy. A clean streak past 3 out-scores any risky grab, and it out-scores any shot.

6. Sharper on every screen

The canvas now renders at device pixel ratio, capped at 2, so sprites are crisp on phones and HiDPI monitors instead of the soft upscale they had before. Every sprite is rasterised once at 256px with a uniform lit-top-left, shaded-bottom-right pass, which gives the fruit a consistent read without per-frame lighting cost. Every emoji in the UI — hearts, trophy, lock, speaker — is now an SVG, so the panel looks the same on every OS instead of borrowing whatever emoji font the device happens to ship.

On PC the mouse is now locked to the canvas while playing. Fast basket moves used to run the cursor off the edge of the game and stall the basket against the wall; pointer lock removes the edge. Esc releases it and absolute tracking resumes.

7. Juice

A caught fruit bursts into four flying quarters and a spray of droplets. A missed one squashes on the floor and leaves a spreading puddle. A dud bomb puffs smoke. The basket throws sparks when you move it fast, and the gun has muzzle sparks and recoil. None of this changes a number, and all of it was added after the movement changes, because faster fruit needs clearer feedback about what just happened to it.

8. Faster on phones

Fruit Frenzy is a one-handed phone game first, and the profiler said the frame was being spent on the wrong things. The ambient decor — drifting stars, background fruit, the little fruit-eater blobs — was costing more per frame than the game underneath it, so it now pauses while you play and resumes on the menus. Canvas shadow blur is limited to the basket, bombs and stars; static gradients are cached per resize; the SVG sprites are pre-rasterised to bitmaps once, which fixes a WebKit habit of re-rasterising SVG on every draw. The header lost its backdrop blur for a solid panel.

Two mobile fixes rode along. Sound on iOS now works — the AudioContext is resumed inside the Start tap, which is the only place iOS allows it. And switching language on the game-over screen no longer replays the game-over sound.

9. Japanese

Fruit Frenzy now plays in English, Korean and Japanese, with Noto Sans JP loaded alongside Nunito for the JA strings. The old external string files are gone; the string table is inline, which also shaved the load.

Personal-best tiers on the play page

The Bronze / Silver / Gold tiers under your best score on the play page were set at 1,000 / 5,000 / 15,000 — numbers written when we assumed a much higher point rate than the game actually has. At one or two points per fruit, Gold was not reachable. The new tiers are 300 / 1,000 / 2,000, which line up with the game’s own score achievements. Your saved best is untouched; only the badge thresholds moved.

How to play v1.3 well

  1. Combo first. Past 3, every fruit is worth double. Nothing the gun does is worth more than keeping that streak alive.
  2. Shoot bombs, never fruit. A shot bomb is +1 and counts as avoided. A shot fruit is −1 life. If you are not sure what it is, do not fire.
  3. Keep one bullet banked for seekers. A bomb leaning into your basket is far easier to pop than to dodge.
  4. Read the spin. Hovering fruit and hovering bombs spin up before they drop. Be underneath the fruit; be away from the bomb.
  5. Take the crate. It costs nothing to miss and a four-bullet bank changes level 6.

Next to the rest of the catalogue

ArcadeDeck has a few games in the one-input-and-a-falling-sky corner. Falling Dodger is the pure dodge version — nothing to catch, everything to avoid. Neon Stack is one tap with the timing running the other way, upward. Fruit Frenzy is the one where the falling things are worth something and the decision is which of them to go under. v1.3 adds a second verb to that decision without replacing the first.

What we are watching

Three things. Whether the two-bullet bank is enough at level 6 and 7 without a crate, or whether the reload needs to scale with level. Whether 30% seeking bombs at level 2 is too early — that is the first level where new players meet fruit that moves, and stacking a hunting bomb on top might be one lesson too many. And whether the earlier miss rule catches any honest catches; the basket’s underside is the line, and if that line is producing losses that look like catches we will move it.

Bug reports and tuning notes go to help@arcadedeck.net. The useful ones name a level and the thing that felt wrong (“level 4 skid fruit landed outside the wall”) rather than general impressions. Patch notes land here.

title: Personal Bests and Mastery Badges: A Score System With No Leaderboard
author: ArcadeDeck Team
coverImageAlt: ArcadeDeck key art — a crystalline open book radiating light, ringed by a gamepad, dice, gems and a star on a dark starfield.
excerpt: Every ArcadeDeck game now remembers your best run and awards a Bronze, Silver or Gold badge for it, and My Games rolls those into a Deck Level. It all lives in your browser: how the score message works, why we removed the leaderboard, and how the tiers are set.
content:
Every game on ArcadeDeck now remembers your best run. Finish a game and the play page shows your personal best, a Bronze, Silver or Gold badge for it, and how far you are from the next one. Over on My Games those badges roll up into a Deck Level for the whole catalogue. None of it leaves your browser. There is no leaderboard, no account, no server, and nothing to submit. This post is what shipped, how it works under the hood, and why we built a score system that is deliberately only about you.

TL;DR

Games post their final score to the site when a run ends. The site keeps the best one in your browser and shows it on the play page with a Bronze / Silver / Gold tier. My Games sums every game you have played, every tier you have earned and your best daily streak into a Deck Level you can share as a line of text. 26 of the 28 playable games take part. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

What you see

On any play page, once you have finished at least one run, a chip under the title reads Best Score: 1,240 — or Best Depth, Best Stage, Best Waves, Best Survival Time, Best AI Wins, whatever that game actually counts. Beat it and the chip flashes New best! in the same session. Next to it, a tier badge if you have crossed the game’s first threshold, and a small 340 to next tier hint if you have not crossed the last one.

On My Games, every game you have played shows its best and its badge, and the top of the page shows your Deck Level: an XP bar, how many games you have played out of the catalogue, how many you have mastered, and your best streak. A Share my deck button copies a one-line summary to the clipboard.

Why there is no leaderboard

ArcadeDeck used to have one. Global rankings, per-game boards and a monthly Hall of Fame all ran for the first few months of the site, and we wrote them up when they were new. We took the whole thing out in July, and the reason is worth being honest about.

A score that arrives from an iframe is a number the browser sent us. Anyone who can open a developer console can send a different number. Making a public board trustworthy means signing scores on a server, validating them against what a run could plausibly produce, watching for macros, and moderating the results by hand when the first two fail — and we ran all of that for a catalogue of small browser games with a team that would rather be shipping the games. Every hour spent policing a leaderboard was an hour not spent on the thing the leaderboard was supposed to be about. On top of that, the board itself made most players feel worse: a top ten is a list of nine people you are not.

So we asked what a score is actually for, if not for ranking strangers. The answer we landed on is that it is for measuring yourself against yesterday. That needs no server, no anti-cheat and no moderation, because the only person you can cheat is you. Personal bests are that answer, built as small as we could make it.

How a score gets from the game to the page

Every hosted game runs in an iframe. When a run ends, the game posts one message to the page around it: a type of GAME_OVER and a score. That is the entire contract, and it is the same for all 26 games — a tower defense reports its peak wave the same way an arcade catcher reports its points.

The site only listens to messages from the game’s own origin, throws away anything that is not a positive finite number, and compares it to the best it already has. If the new run is higher, it stores it under a per-game key in localStorage and flips the chip. If it is not, nothing happens. There is no network request in that path at all. You could play every game on the site with the connection cut after the first load and your bests would still update.

Two kinds of game needed a different shape. Hot-seat games — Omok, Tank Battle, Spirit Duel — only report wins against the AI, counted cumulatively, because a score from two people sharing a keyboard is not a score for either of them. Idle games — AshenKeys, Debt & Dragons, Entrepreneur Tycoon — have no game over to hook, so they post a heartbeat every five seconds and once more when the tab closes, and the site keeps the highest one it saw. Triangle Battle is the one playable game that sits this out: it is hot-seat only, and there is no AI to count wins against.

Tiers

Each participating game carries three ascending thresholds. Cross the first and the chip turns Bronze; the second, Silver; the third, Gold. A Gold game counts as mastered on My Games. The thresholds are set per game against what that game actually measures:

  • Gate of Hell — Depth 10 / 25 / 50.
  • Skyfall — Survival Time 30 / 60 / 120 seconds.
  • Polygon Invasion TD — Peak Wave 10 / 25 / 50.
  • Entrepreneur Tycoon — Money Earned $10,000 / $100,000 / $1,000,000.
  • Mythic Defenders — Stage 1 / 2 / 3. Three stages is the whole campaign; clearing it is Gold.
  • Fruit Frenzy — Score 300 / 1,000 / 2,000.

The intent for every game is the same: Bronze is a session where you understood the game, Silver is a session where you were good at it, Gold is a session someone who plays a lot would be pleased with. The thresholds are a tuning knob, not a promise. Fruit Frenzy’s first set was 1,000 / 5,000 / 15,000, written before we checked that the game pays one or two points per fruit; Gold was not reachable, and we moved it in the v1.3 notes. If a tier turns out to be trivially easy or effectively impossible we will move it, and your saved best is never touched when we do — only the badge it earns.

It lives in your browser, so it lives in one browser

Bests, played history and streaks are stored in localStorage. They do not follow you from your phone to your desktop, and clearing site data wipes them. That is the trade for having no account. If you want your Deck Level to survive a browser reset, the share line is a screenshot-sized record of it.

Deck Level

My Games rolls everything into one number. The formula is small enough to print:

  • 10 XP for every game you have played at least once.
  • 25 XP for every tier earned — so a Gold game is worth 75 on top of its 10 for being played.
  • 5 XP for every day in your best daily play streak.
  • 100 XP per level.

Playing everything once gets you to level 3. Mastering the catalogue gets you past level 20. The streak term is deliberately the smallest; it is there so that showing up counts for something, not so that a calendar can out-earn a Gold run.

A score is for measuring yourself against yesterday. That needs no server, because the only person you can cheat is you.

What it is not

It is not a leaderboard and it is not going to quietly become one. The message every game posts also carries a secondary stat we are not using yet, and the contract was written so that a global ranking could hook the same message without touching any game again. That is a door left unlocked, not a plan. If we ever walk through it, it will be because we have found a way to run a public board that does not cost more than it gives back, and it will be opt-in.

It is also not an achievement system in the individual games. Several of them have their own — Fruit Frenzy tracks fifty, Ashen Keys has its own ascension tree — and those stay inside the game. The site-level system only asks one question of each game: what is the number you are proudest of, and how big was it this time.

What we are watching

Two things. First, tier placement: we set 26 sets of thresholds mostly from the games’ own achievement tables and our own runs, and some will be wrong in one direction or the other. Second, whether the heartbeat approach for idle games produces bests that feel earned; a number that ticks up while a tab sits open is a different kind of score from one you fought for, and if the Deck Level ends up dominated by idle Golds we will weight it.

If a tier feels off, help@arcadedeck.net is the place — name the game, your best, and which badge you think it should have earned. Patch notes land here.

title: Flux Tower Defense: Free Web Edition, Waves 1–10
author: ArcadeDeck Team
coverImageAlt: Flux Tower Defense key art — glowing towers walling a snaking path across a dark grid as polygonal enemies march from a red portal toward a teal fortress.
excerpt: Flux Tower Defense is now free in the browser: the first ten waves of the Steam game with the full random loadout draft, Lv 1–15 upgrades, elemental attributes, evolutions, elite modifiers and clickable disasters. What the web edition includes, what stays on Steam, and how to clear wave 10.
content:
Flux Tower Defense is now playable on ArcadeDeck, free, in the browser. When it landed on Steam in May we said there would be no web edition. That changed. The play page now hosts the first ten waves of the real game — same board, same random loadout draft, same Lv 1–15 upgrade path, same disasters — and the run ends with a clear screen and a link to the full release. This post is what the web edition contains, what it deliberately leaves out, and how to actually get through wave 10 with the fortress standing.

TL;DR

Grid tower defense on a 19×15 board with no fixed lane: towers block, traps sit on the path, and the route recomputes the moment you place or sell anything. Every run drafts a random loadout from 40 towers and 15 traps. Lv 5 rolls an attribute (LAVA / GLACIER / ELECTRIC / STEEL), Lv 10 unlocks Tier 2, Lv 15 can attempt an Evolution. Ten elite modifiers, a boss every wave from the second, clickable natural disasters, tollgates, three difficulties and a Daily Challenge. Web edition = waves 1–10, saved in your browser, 11 languages, PC only. Personal best on the play page is waves cleared; a full clear is Diamond.

The maze is the game

There is no lane. Enemies leave a red portal and walk the shortest walkable route to your teal fortress, and that route is recomputed every single time the board changes. Towers are walls. Where you put them is the map. Wall Towers exist only to bend the path — they are the cheapest cell on the board and they do not shoot. Every other tower shoots, but it also blocks, so a damage tower placed in the wrong cell can shorten the route it was supposed to guard.

Traps are the mirror image. They sit on the route rather than beside it, do nothing to pathing, and fire when something walks over them. Tollgates work the same way but for economy: mortgage a stretch of path for gold, and whoever crosses it gets a speed buff as the price. The game refuses any placement that would seal the fortress off completely and warns you, so you cannot brick a run by accident — but you can absolutely open a shortcut by selling the wrong wall. Right-click sells, and the path snaps to the new opening before the next enemy takes a step.

You do not pick your build

Every run drafts a loadout at random from 40 towers, auras and specials plus 15 traps. There is no shop menu where you pick your favourites; you plan around what you drew, and every five waves you draft one reward on top. Two runs with the same map play completely differently because the arsenal is different, and the corridor you build should be different too. A loadout with Frost Plate and Tesla Coil wants a long slow corridor where chains and slows stack; one with Blade Launcher and Tar Pit wants a tight loop past a single kill zone.

Upgrades are where the depth is. Each tower levels from 1 to 15. Lv 4 and Lv 9 are per-tower enhancements. Lv 5 rolls an attribute — LAVA, GLACIER, ELECTRIC or STEEL — that changes how the tower behaves and how it looks. Lv 10 upgrades it to Tier 2 (burn, freeze, chain, crit, depending on the roll). Lv 15 rolls a second attribute. Four towers can attempt an Evolution at max level: a 60% roll that either transforms the tower or knocks it back to Lv 4. Towers also bank kills toward veterancy ranks, and Tier 3 veterancy unlocks a permanent perk pick.

The waves push back

Every wave from the second carries a boss. Regular enemies can spawn with one of ten elite modifiers — Haste, Shielded, Armored, Juggernaut, Regen, Phasing, EMP, Frenzied, Vampiric, Phoenix — and some species carry permanent passives like Fireproof or Burrow on top. Between waves a natural disaster can land: meteor, blizzard, earthquake, tornado, thunderstorm. Each one has a hotspot and a timer, and you click the hotspot down before the timer runs out or it takes a tower with it. The towers under a disaster you ignore are the price of ignoring it.

Three difficulties change enemy HP, gold income, starting life and the wall cap. The Daily Challenge hands everyone the same map and the same loadout for one attempt per day, which is the closest thing the web edition has to a shared scoreboard.

What the web edition is, and is not

The web build ends after wave 10 with the fortress standing. That is the proving run. Everything inside those ten waves is the real thing: every difficulty, the full random draft, the whole Lv 1–15 path with attributes and Tier 2 abilities, evolutions, veterancy, elite modifiers, disasters, tollgates and the Daily Challenge. The run auto-saves in your browser at every wave clear and on pause, and the main menu offers Continue. It ships with 11 in-game languages including English, Korean and Japanese.

What it does not have is everything that happens after wave 10. The Steam release is the full game: endless waves, a second portal that opens at wave 10 and more after it, the Challenger boss, and the New Discovery content — two more elements (VOID and BLIGHT), the reroll-only apex element SUPERIOR, Prisma currency to reroll a tower's attribute, and five Power-Up star tiers past Lv 15. The web edition shows those slots locked in the menu but never generates any of it. Steam also has 20 achievements, all-time / weekly / daily leaderboards and cloud saves; the web save does not carry over.

PC only

The board needs right-click to sell, drag to lay walls and a hover-driven detail panel, and the 19×15 grid is laid out for a desktop screen. There is no touch layout, and we are not planning one for this title. Play it on a computer.

Personal best on the play page

Flux Tower Defense reports waves cleared to the play page, so your personal best is the highest wave you have finished. The tiers are short because the run is short: Bronze at 3 waves, Silver at 5, Gold at 8, and a full 10-wave clear is Diamond — the cap and the top tier are the same number, so beating the web edition once is the whole ladder. The Tiers tab on the play page shows the full table.

How to clear wave 10

  • Build the maze first, the damage second. Spend the opening gold on Wall Towers and draw one long, snaking corridor past a single spot. Then put a tower in that spot.
  • Read the loadout before placing anything. Press Q, W and E and look at what you drew. Slows and chains want length; burst wants a loop that passes the same cell twice.
  • One carry to Lv 5 early. A single tower at Lv 5 with an attribute roll out-damages six towers at Lv 3, and it is the tower you will push to Tier 2 at Lv 10.
  • Click the disaster. When a hotspot appears, stop what you are doing and click it down. The timer is short and the tower under it is not coming back.
  • Sell to reroute. A boss past your kill zone is not lost yet. Right-click a wall, open a new turn, and the path updates instantly. Z undoes a placement for five seconds if you open the wrong one.
  • Space on a selected tower smart-upgrades it. On an empty selection it starts the next wave. Do not press it by reflex with a tower selected unless you meant to spend the gold.
  • Keep gold for wave 10. On Steam a second portal opens there; in the web edition wave 10 is still the heaviest wave, and a reroute costs walls.

Next to the other tower defenses

ArcadeDeck now hosts four TDs and they barely overlap. Polygon Invasion TD is a fixed-lane build with eight towers and 24 evolutions, where the lane is given and the puzzle is the order you upgrade in. Mythic Defenders: Heroes Returns replaces towers with drafted heroes and merge tiers on a 10×10 board. Barrack Defense has no towers at all — you build barracks and the units they train fight on their own. Flux is the one where the map is yours to draw, which makes it the closest to classic maze-building TD and the furthest from the other three.

What we are watching

Whether the 60% Evolution roll reads as a gamble or a trap when it drops a Lv 15 tower back to Lv 4 in the middle of wave 9 — the intent is a gamble. Whether the disaster timers are fair at the hardest difficulty, where a tornado on a Lv 10 carry is effectively a run loss.
