And how many people finish wave 10 on their first run; the tiers on the play page assume most do not, and if the Diamond rate is high the middle of the ladder moves.

Bug reports and feedback go to help@arcadedeck.net — tag the subject [FLUX] for routing. The useful ones name a wave and a specific decision (“the tollgate on wave 6 buffed the boss past my only chain tower”) rather than general impressions. Ten waves is the proving run. What comes after is on Steam.

title: Mythic Defenders v6.4: Five New Heroes, Pause & Continue, and Phones
author: ArcadeDeck Team
coverImageAlt: Mythic Defenders: Heroes Returns key art — mythic heroes guarding a grid battlefield against corrupted monsters.
excerpt: Mythic Defenders: Heroes Returns v6.4 adds Kali, Maui, Saraswati, Baba Yaga and Oya (50 heroes), five new monsters, a tactical pause, Continue from the last wave, a full phone layout and a rebuilt D Dorian soundtrack. What changed, how the new monsters work, and a correction to our May post.
content:
Mythic Defenders: Heroes Returns just got its biggest build since launch. Version 6.4 is live on the play page: five new heroes, five new monsters, a tactical pause, a Continue button that survives closing the tab, a full mobile pass and a sound engine rebuilt from scratch. This post is what changed, what it means for how you play, and a few habits that make the new monsters less painful.

TL;DR

Deck-building tower defense on a 10×10 grid: build a deck of 5–10 heroes from a roster of 50, clear 3 stages of 5 waves with a boss every fifth wave. New in 6.4: Kali, Maui, Saraswati, Baba Yaga and Oya; Gilded Rat, Ironshell Scarab, Storm Ram, Hourglass Weaver and Marsh Lantern; pause with Esc / P / ⏸; the run saves at every wave boundary; the full board now fits phones and tablets in landscape. ArcadeDeck tracks the stage you reach — clear all three for Diamond.

A correction first

Our May launch post described banked mana, a widening card pool and a PC-only build. None of that matches the game. There is no mana economy: you spend essence, the cost of each summon climbs by 5, and the deck you curate is the pool. The game has also run on touch for a while, and 6.4 makes phones properly playable. The catalogue copy was rewritten against the real build in the same update.

How a run actually works

Every summon opens FATE DRAWS: three cards from your deck are revealed and you keep one. Costs go 10, 15, 20… and the 45 starting essence covers exactly the first three, which the wave timer waits 10 seconds for. Drag the hero onto any buildable cell. Drop it onto a copy of the same hero at the same tier to merge it to tier 2, then tier 3. Kills level a hero separately; at level 9 it evolves for +30% ATK, +20% attack speed, +10% crit and an upgraded ability. Regret a placement? The Portal to Heaven in the corner refunds 70%.

Elements do not counter enemies — they buff your own side. Pantheon Bond is locked in when the run starts from your deck's breadth and depth; Field Resonance is live, giving each hero ATK and attack speed for every same-element hero on the grid. Two or three of one element beats one of each.

Five new heroes, 50 total

Kali, Maui, Saraswati, Baba Yaga and Oya join the roster, each with a level-9 evolution and a cast of their own. Kali, the Dancer of Endings, is the one you will notice first: Dance of Destruction opens with a slash and then spins four blades around her for a few seconds, cutting everything they sweep through. New recruits come from the same place as always — 60 Mythic Coins rolls a hero, and a duplicate plus 40 coins powers one up permanently.

Five new monsters, and how to handle them

The bestiary is now 20 monster types in normal, elite and boss forms. The new five each break a habit:

  • Gilded Rat — frail, fast, carrying 3–4× normal essence. It bolts for the exit; kill it early or lose the payday. Its elite form is the Rat King.
  • Ironshell Scarab — shrugs off a flat chunk of every hit. Many small hits do little; fewer, heavier hits (merged tier-3s, evolved abilities) do the work.
  • Storm Ram — builds speed until something hits it. Any hit resets the charge, so put it in range early and keep touching it.
  • Hourglass Weaver — rewinds its own HP once at 35%. Chip damage wastes the rewind on you; burst it through the threshold.
  • Marsh Lantern — hastens everything around it, and it flies. Ground-only heroes ignore it.

The last point is the one that ends runs. Heroes are ground, air or both — the mound / wing icon on each plate tells you which. Keep at least one air-capable hero on the board by wave 2.

Pause, and Continue

Press Esc, P or the ⏸ button to freeze enemies, heroes, timers and projectiles. The sidebars stay readable, so you can check the bestiary and plan the next merge with the clock stopped. Close the tab mid-run and the title screen now offers Continue: the run is saved at every wave boundary, so you replay the current wave with your board, essence and lives intact.

Built for phones now

The grid sizes itself between the two sidebars, so the full 10×10 board fits phones, tablets and 1366×768 laptops in landscape. FATE DRAWS sits above the sidebars, cards open their ability text on tap via the ⓘ badge, the result screen scrolls, and the layout respects notches and home bars. Performance got the same attention: on a 16-hero board, frame time dropped from about 6.4 ms to 0.7 ms, which matters most on mid-range phones.

It looks and sounds different

Merged heroes wear bronze / silver / gold plates with ★ badges, so tiers read at a glance. Enemies have darker rims against the board, skill casts draw rune sigils with shockwaves and a short freeze-frame, and the pixel art renders 1:1. Everything you hear is synthesised at runtime in D Dorian: 25 sound cues, a different attack timbre per element, and a soundtrack that shifts between menu, combat and boss moods. The speaker control in the corner of every screen has separate effects and music sliders.

Fixes worth knowing about

Hero abilities now fire before max level — a bug had limited them to evolved heroes. Kill credit lands exactly once. If a hero felt weak in earlier builds, try it again.

Build a deck, start a run, and see how far the pantheon holds. If you like the genre, Flux Tower Defense and Barrack Defense take it in very different directions.

title: Trade Tycoon Launch: Twelve Cities, Five Eras, One Floating Island
author: ArcadeDeck Team
coverImageAlt: Trade Tycoon key art — a floating island of glowing cities linked by roads and rivers at night.
excerpt: Trade Tycoon is live: grow 8 of 12 cities on a floating night island from tribal camps to industrial powers. How eras and score work, hidden building synergies, caravan trade and auto trade, the branching objective tree, and a solid first hour.
content:
Trade Tycoon is live. Our newest original is a city-building and trade strategy game set on a floating island at night: twelve settlements, eight of them yours, four run by rival towns you can only barter with. Start every city as a tribal camp of 100 people and push it through five eras to an industrial power. It is on the play page now, on phone, tablet and desktop, and installs as an app that plays offline.

TL;DR

Run 8 of 12 cities (4 random NPC rivals each game), 22 buildings, dozens of hidden building synergies, caravan trade routes along roads and rivers, and a branching objective tree where every path ends in a 🏆 win. Score = each city's population × its era multiplier. ArcadeDeck tracks your best score — Bronze starts at 5,000, Diamond sits at 5,000,000.

What you are actually doing

Every city has its own terrain — coastal, forest, mountain, farming, desert or trade — and one of three possible specialties, rolled fresh each game. Open a city, queue buildings, and let it grow. There is no single capital to protect and no army to manage: the whole game is getting food, materials and knowledge to the right place at the right time.

Each city climbs the eras on its own schedule, and it needs both a population goal and a total knowledge goal to do it:

  • Ancient — 200 people, 50 knowledge (2× score)
  • Medieval — 1,000 people, 300 knowledge (5×)
  • Renaissance — 5,000 people, 1,500 knowledge (10×)
  • Industrial — 15,000 people, 5,000 knowledge (20×)

That table is the whole score model. A Tribal city of 1,000 is worth 1,000 points; the same 1,000 people in the Medieval era are worth 5,000. Gold does not score, and NPC cities do not count. So the question every few minutes is simple: which of my cities is closest to its next era, and what is it short of?

Buildings and synergies

Twenty-two building types unlock by era — Farms, Fisheries, Sawmills and Quarries from the start; Iron Mines, Workshops and Breweries in the Ancient era; Gold Mines and Foundries later; Factories only once a city goes Industrial. Knowledge comes from Schoolhouses, Libraries and Academies. Some buildings carry upkeep (a Brewery eats food, a Foundry burns stone and wood), so a new building can quietly flip a surplus into a shortage.

Buildings also affect each other. A Warehouse next to Farms preserves more food; Schoolhouses feed Libraries; a Merchant Guild makes a Market more profitable. Not every pairing is friendly: a Quarry's dust and noise cut Farm harvests, and an Iron Mine's runoff pollutes the soil. The in-game manual lists each synergy only after you have discovered it, so half the fun of a second game is finding the ones you missed.

Trade is the engine

A city with a Market, Bazaar or Merchant Guild can open trade routes. Caravans follow roads and rivers across the map, and distance, guilds, ports and terrain decide what a route earns. You do not have to micromanage every crate: auto trade moves surpluses between your own cities to wherever something is short. NPC cities are different — each has a Looking for / Selling board, and you barter with what they want.

Hub city

A Merchant Guild earns 1.5× on every route that runs through it. Pick one well-connected city, put the Guild there, and route through it. River cities (🌊) get extra food and gold and are the only ones that can build a Port — they make natural hubs.

The objective tree

Instead of a fixed victory condition, Trade Tycoon gives you a tree of objectives. Finish one, confirm it, and the next ones open. At a ◆ choice node you commit to one branch and the others close for the rest of the game. Every branch ends in a 🏆 winning objective, so there is no wrong path — just different games. Read what a choice closes before you confirm it.

A solid first hour

  1. Food first. Get a Farm or two in every city so food stays positive and population keeps rising. Negative food stalls everything.
  2. Knowledge early. A Schoolhouse in each city from the start. Population without knowledge will not change eras, and eras are where the score is.
  3. Warehouses before big builds. Storage caps decide what you can afford; the Medieval-era buildings cost more than a small camp can hold.
  4. Market in every city. Then let auto trade even out shortages while you focus on the city nearest its next era.
  5. Watch the neighbours. Before placing a Quarry or Iron Mine, check what is next to your Farms.

Also in the box

A first-time tutorial, a full in-game manual, city hotkeys (1–8, rebindable), 1× / 2× speed, pan and zoom, long-press tooltips on touch, and English, Korean and Japanese text. Music and effects are written in D Dorian with a volume control, and M mutes.

If you like slow-burn economy games, Entrepreneur Tycoon and Galaxy Launch scratch the same itch in a different key. Otherwise: open Trade Tycoon, build a Farm, and see how far one campfire goes.
